prompt:
Scope (backend only): implement removal of the title property from every public API response that returns entry objects; continue to reject incoming requests that include a title property with HTTP 422; do not rename or alter the database column named "title"; do not change representation or behavior of description, id, owner_id, created_at fields.

Concrete implementation tasks:

1) Find all entry response producers
- Search the codebase for all serializers/DTOs/response builders/templates that produce entry objects (single and collection responses), including but not limited to: GET /entries, GET /entries/{id}, search/list endpoints, bulk export endpoints, webhooks, streaming endpoints, CSV/JSON export endpoints, any endpoints returning embedded/nested entry objects.
- Identify every place where the field named "title" is read from a model and included in an outgoing public response.

2) Stop exposing title in public responses
- For every serializer/response DTO that currently includes title, remove title from the response shape so the public JSON no longer contains a "title" key. Do not change the name of the DB column or the ORM/model attribute; only remove the property from the serialized output.
- Ensure the entry response still includes "name" (only output name), and that name is populated as before. If any serializer previously used title as the exported name, change it to use the model's name attribute explicitly.
- Ensure description, id, owner_id, created_at remain present and unchanged in format and datatype in every response where they currently appear.

3) Validation of incoming requests (create/update/patch/etc.)
- For all request handlers that accept entry payloads (create, update, patch or bulk operations), enforce validation that the request body MUST NOT contain the key "title". If a client submits a payload containing a title key (any value), return HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity.
- Implement the 422 response consistently across handlers, using your standard validation/error response format. Example canonical response body to use as template (adapt to existing error schema):
  HTTP 422
  Content-Type: application/json
  {
    "errors": [
      {
        "field": "title",
        "code": "forbidden",
        "message": "'title' is not allowed in requests"
      }
    ]
  }
- If your validation framework allows explicit "forbidden"/"disallowed" properties in the schema, add title as forbidden so the framework itself returns 422; otherwise add an explicit validation rule early in the request pipeline that checks for presence of title and returns the 422 above.

4) API schema and docs
- Update OpenAPI / JSON Schema / API documentation for the backend so that:
  - Responses that describe entry objects no longer list "title" as a property. They must list "name" and the other unchanged properties (description, id, owner_id, created_at, etc.).
  - Request bodies that accept entry objects must not accept "title"; mark it as disallowed/forbidden in schema where the schema language supports it and/or note that requests containing title will be rejected with 422.
- Do not change the DB column name in schemas or DB migrations. Document that the internal DB column remains named "title" but is not exposed in responses.

5) Tests
- Add/modify automated tests to assert the new behavior:
  - Unit tests for serializers/response builders: given an Entry model with title set, serialized output must NOT contain "title" and must contain "name" and the unchanged fields (id, description, owner_id, created_at) with identical formatting.
  - Integration/API tests: GET endpoints returning entries (single and collection) must not include "title" in the JSON body.
  - Request validation tests: POST/PUT/PATCH endpoints must return 422 when the request body contains a "title" key. Assert the response uses the standard validation error format and includes field="title" or equivalent indicator.
  - Tests for export/webhook endpoints: ensure exported payloads and webhook payloads do not include "title".

6) Code reviews and scanning
- Search for occurrences where responses are assembled outside of serializer code (manual JSON assembly, template rendering, logging surfaced to clients) and remove title from those outputs.
- Scan caching layers, CDN responses, pre-generated export files, and background jobs for any public outputs that may still carry title; adjust those producers to not include title.
- Do not change internal logging/audit storage schema unless those logs are publicly accessible; if logs are public-facing, ensure they do not expose title.

7) Back-end-only coordination notes (do not instruct front-end changes)
- The backend must stop sending title in any public response. At the same time, the backend must keep rejecting incoming requests that include title with 422. These two facts are binding acceptance criteria and must both be implemented by the backend.

8) Acceptance criteria (explicit checks for QA)
- All public API responses that return entries: no "title" key present; "name" is present and unchanged; id, description, owner_id, created_at are present and unchanged in format.
- Any request containing a title key receives HTTP 422 with a validation-error body referencing title.
- Database column/ORM attribute named "title" remains present and unchanged (no renames or migrations altering its name).
- Exports, webhooks, and any other externally-visible payloads are updated to omit title.

9) Rollback and monitoring
- Deploy with feature-flag or run tests in staging to verify that no public response contains title and that 422 behavior for requests is enforced before promoting to production.
- Monitor error logs for unexpected 422 spikes; instrument a one-time metric for requests containing title to detect remaining callers.

Do not change any database column names or storage formats. Do not assume any front-end changes—implement the backend rules and schema/docs changes above so the API no longer exposes title and rejects incoming title in requests.
